claim: 3D microanatomical characterization of the 380-million-year-old lobe-finned fish Eusthenopteron revealed longitudinally-oriented trabeculae within the shaft of their humeri.
source: Confirming previous observations (Sanchez et al., 2014; Sanchez et al., 2016), 3D microanatomical characterization of the 380-million-year-old lobe-finned fish Eusthenopteron revealed longitudinally-oriented trabeculae within the shaft of their humeri (Figure 1A)
evidence: Supported by synchrotron scanning data presented in Figure 1A and cited previous studies

claim: Longitudinally-oriented trabeculae in Eusthenopteron strongly indicate that endochondral ossification facilitates bone elongation in stem tetrapods in a manner similar to that in stem amniotes and present-day mammals.
source: 3D microanatomical characterization of the 380-million-year-old lobe-finned fish Eusthenopteron revealed longitudinally-oriented trabeculae within the shaft of their humeri (Figure 1A), strongly indicating that endochondral ossification facilitates bone elongation in stem tetrapods in a manner similar to that in stem amniotes (290 Mya) (e.g., Seymouria, Figure 1B) and present-day mammals (e.g., red squirrel, Figure 1C).
evidence: Based on inference from comparative anatomical data across evolutionary taxa shown in Figures 1A-C

claim: The SOC is not present in anamniotes and first appears in amniotes.
source: Evolutionary analysis revealed that the SOC is not present in anamniotes and first appears in amniotes, animals that relocate their entire lifecycle on land (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis presented in Figure 1D

claim: Amniotes are animals that relocate their entire lifecycle on land.
source: Evolutionary analysis revealed that the SOC is not present in anamniotes and first appears in amniotes, animals that relocate their entire lifecycle on land (Figure 1D).
evidence: Based on established biological knowledge about amniote characteristics

claim: Among various groups of synapsids, the SOC is present in all crown mammals.
source: Among various groups of synapsids, the SOC is present in all crown mammals, whereas some stem mammals have evolved a SOC [i.e., Niassodon (Castanhinha et al., 2013; Figure 1D)] but others have not (Chinsamy and Abdala, 2008; Ray and Chinsamy, 2004).
evidence: Supported by cited literature and phylogenetic data in Figure 1D

claim: Some stem mammals have evolved a SOC, such as Niassodon, but others have not.
source: Among various groups of synapsids, the SOC is present in all crown mammals, whereas some stem mammals have evolved a SOC [i.e., Niassodon (Castanhinha et al., 2013; Figure 1D)] but others have not (Chinsamy and Abdala, 2008; Ray and Chinsamy, 2004).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited studies on stem mammal ossification patterns

claim: Lepidosauria generally develops a SOC (lizards) or calcified secondary center (sphenodontids).
source: Lepidosauria generally develops a SOC (lizards) or calcified secondary center (SC, sphenodontids) (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by phylogenetic analysis in Figure 1D

claim: Archosauria does not develop SOCs or calcified secondary centers, with the exception of few bones with SOCs in some birds.
source: However, Archosauria does not develop such structures [(Haines, 1938), Figure 1D] with the exception of few bones with SOCs in some birds (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by cited literature and imaging data in Figures 1D and 1E

claim: Archosauria develops bone marrow protrusions with calcified or ossified walls that protrude into the epiphyseal cartilage and sequester the hypertrophic chondrocytes in between them.
source: Instead, this clade develops bone marrow protrusions with calcified or ossified walls that protrude into the epiphyseal cartilage and sequester the hypertrophic chondrocytes in between them (Haines, 1938; Haines, 1942; Barreto et al., 1993; Horner et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited studies on archosaur bone development

claim: Ossified protrusions are relatively small in chelonians and crocodilians and quite extended in birds and non-avian dinosaurs.
source: These ossified protrusions are relatively small in chelonians and crocodilians and quite extended in birds and non-avian dinosaurs (Haines, 1938; Haines, 1942; Chinsamy and Abdala, 2008; Ray and Chinsamy, 2004 and Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by cited literature and imaging data in Figure 1E

claim: The weight-bearing bones of certain birds exhibit a SOC together with ossified protrusions.
source: Although the weight-bearing bones of certain birds exhibit a SOC together with such protrusions (e.g., the proximal epiphysis of the tibiotarsus in sparrow Figure 1E), most ossify without forming a SOC (Horner et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by cited literature and imaging data showing sparrow tibiotarsus in Figure 1E

claim: Most bird bones ossify without forming a SOC.
source: Although the weight-bearing bones of certain birds exhibit a SOC together with such protrusions (e.g., the proximal epiphysis of the tibiotarsus in sparrow Figure 1E), most ossify without forming a SOC (Horner et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by cited literature on bird bone ossification patterns

claim: Anamniotes spend their juvenile growth period in an aquatic environment.
source: It has to be emphasized that anamniotes spend their juvenile growth period in an aquatic environment, with amniotes being the first to translocate their entire life cycle on land.
evidence: Based on established biological knowledge about anamniote life cycles

claim: Amniotes are the first to translocate their entire life cycle on land.
source: It has to be emphasized that anamniotes spend their juvenile growth period in an aquatic environment, with amniotes being the first to translocate their entire life cycle on land.
evidence: Based on established evolutionary biology knowledge

claim: The habitat change from aquatic to terrestrial may pose additional mechanical demands on the growing skeleton.
source: Such habitat change may pose additional mechanical demands on the growing skeleton, which must be sufficiently rigid to bear the body weight during a wide range of movements, yet flexible enough to allow bone elongation.
evidence: Based on logical inference about mechanical requirements of terrestrial locomotion

claim: The growing skeleton must be sufficiently rigid to bear the body weight during a wide range of movements, yet flexible enough to allow bone elongation.

source: Accordingly, we next hypothesized that the development of the SOC or ossified protrusions might be viewed as skeletal adaptations to the weight-bearing demands of the terrestrial environment and associated mechanical stresses posed on the epiphyseal cartilage.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on evolutionary observations

claim: The SOC significantly enhances the stiffness of the entire epiphyseal structure.

claim: The SOC prevents severe distortion and consequent instability during locomotion.
source: First, the FEA showed that the SOC significantly enhances the stiffness of the entire epiphyseal structure (note the level of deflection in Figure 1F), thereby preventing severe distortion and consequent instability during locomotion.

claim: FEA provides experimental support to the idea proposed by Haines, 1942.

claim: The presence of either a SOC or ossified protrusions reduces the extent of octahedral shear stress distribution within the region of the epiphyseal plate, particularly where the hypertrophic chondrocytes are located.
source: Furthermore, FEA revealed that the presence of either a SOC or ossified protrusions reduces the extent of octahedral shear stress distribution (associated with either a vertical or an angled load, the latter mimicking locomotion) within the region of the epiphyseal plate, particularly where the hypertrophic chondrocytes are located (Figure 1F, see other stresses in Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Despite being similarly protective for epiphyseal chondrocytes, the ossified protrusions do not improve the stiffness of the joint structure.

claim: Mathematical modeling indicates that both SOC and ossified protrusions reduce octahedral stress within the epiphyseal cartilage, plausibly representing alternative evolutionary strategies for achieving the same goal.

claim: In newborn bats the SOC development in the legs and thumbs of wings is more advanced than in the rest of the wing bones.

claim: The heterochrony in bat ossification was apparent during ontogenesis and consistent within the Chiroptera order.

claim: There is variation of ossification among Chiroptera species, which likely reflects their varying foraging and roosting ecology, behavior of juvenile bats, litter size, and lifespan.

claim: SOCs in the feet and the thumbs of some bat species are well-developed even before birth.

claim: The pups of certain bat species (Mops condylurus, Artibeus jamaicensis, Megaloglossus woermani, and Rousettus celebensis) are born with fully ossified feet of adult size.
source: and the pups of certain species (Mops condylurus, Artibeus jamaicensis, Megaloglossus woermani, and Rousettus celebensis) are born with fully ossified feet of adult size (Adams and Thibault, 2000; Koyabu and Son, 2014) (see also Figure 2B for A. jamaicensis).

claim: Bipedal three-toed jerboa (Jaculus jaculus) jump on their hindlimbs when adult but during the first 2–3 weeks of life they employ only forelimbs thereafter becoming quadrupedal and eventually bipedal.

These animals jump on their hindlimbs when adult but during the first 2–3 weeks of life they employ only forelimbs thereafter becoming quadrupedal and eventually bipedal (Eilam and Shefer, 1997).

claim: SOC formation in the front limbs of Jaculus jaculus significantly preceded the one in the hind limbs.

claim: The development of the SOC coincides with the changes in gait pattern from crawling to walking in mice and rats.

claim: In both Chiroptera and jerboa, advanced ossification is observed in limbs subjected to mechanical duties early in life.
source: Thus, in both Chiroptera and jerboa, advanced ossification is observed in limbs subjected to mechanical duties early in life, which is further strengthening an association between mechanical demands and SOC development.

claim: The association between mechanical demands and SOC development is strengthened by observations in Chiroptera and jerboa.
source: Thus, in both Chiroptera and jerboa, advanced ossification is observed in limbs subjected to mechanical duties early in life, which is further strengthening an association between mechanical demands and SOC development.
evidence: Based on inference from comparative anatomical observations

claim: The absence of terrestrial-associated loading conditions would release the evolutionary pressure on SOC and it can be lost or reduced with time.
source: If demand for SOC is mechanically related, we further reasoned that the absence of terrestrial-associated loading conditions would release the evolutionary pressure on SOC and that it can be lost or reduced with time.

claim: In early cetaceans from the Eocene epoch, the epiphyseal plates of the forelimbs are structurally similar to those of terrestrial mammals, as evident in semi-aquatic Maiacetus inuus and fully aquatic Dorudon atrox, where SOCs are present at the joints connecting carpal bones, metacarpal bones, and phalanges.
source: In early cetaceans from the Eocene epoch (56–33.9 Mya), the epiphyseal plates of the forelimbs are structurally similar to those of terrestrial mammals, as evident in semi-aquatic Maiacetus inuus (Gingerich et al., 2009) and fully aquatic Dorudon atrox (Form, 2004), where SOCs are present at the joints connecting carpal bones, metacarpal bones, and phalanges (Figure 4B 1-2).

claim: In baleen whales (both extant and some extinct from Miocene epoch), there is a clear reduction of SOCs.

claim: In the Balaenopteridae family, SOC is reduced by up to 80% in metacarpals and phalanges.
source: However, in baleen whales (both extant and some extinct from Miocene epoch, 23–5.3 Mya), there is a clear reduction of SOCs such as in the Balaenopteridae family where SOC is reduced by up to 80% in metacarpals and phalanges (Figure 4B 3)

claim: The return of cetaceans to the aquatic environment is associated with a gradual reduction in the size of SOC in a few phylogenetic lineages, and even their complete loss in some species.
